o: We must return each (employee, project) allocation whose workload is strictly greater than the average workload of all projects belonging to employees on that employee's team. The average is computed per team over all rows in Project joined to Employees by team. In the example, Team A's rows have workloads 45 and 68 (avg 56.5), so only Doe's 68 qualifies; Team B's rows are 90 and 12 (avg 51), so only Ali's 90 qualifies. Since table sizes are small and this is a per-group comparison problem, either a window function or a self-join against team averages works. Output columns are employee_id, project_id, employee_name, project_workload, ordered by employee_id then project_id.
k: The comparison baseline is the average workload across ALL project rows of an employee's team, not just that employee's own rows.
A window function AVG(workload) OVER (PARTITION BY team) computes the team average without collapsing rows.
Strictly greater-than ('>') matters: workloads exactly equal to the team average are excluded.

a.i: Join Project with Employees, attach each row's team average using AVG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY team), then filter rows where workload exceeds that average. This reads naturally as 'compare each row to its group's statistic' and avoids any self-join.
s: Join Project p with Employees e on employee_id to get each allocation's team and name.
Compute team_avg = AVG(p.workload) OVER (PARTITION BY e.team).
Select employee_id, project_id, name AS employee_name, workload AS project_workload.

a.i: First materialize the average workload per team from the joined tables, then join allocations back to these averages and keep only those strictly above their team's mean. This is the classic pre-window-function pattern and works even on old SQL dialects.

Join Project p to Employees e on employee_id.

w: In an interview, lead with the window-function approach: it is concise, single-pass, and idiomatic modern SQL; fall back to the CTE join if the interviewer asks about pre-8.0 MySQL compatibility. Common pitfalls: averaging only the employee's own rows instead of the whole team, forgetting to join Employees before grouping (team lives there), using '>=' instead of strict '>', and mislabeling output columns (employee_name, project_workload). Edge cases: teams with a single member always fail the strict '>' test since nothing exceeds its own group's only value... actually a lone member equals the average, so they are excluded. Follow-ups may ask for median workload per team or top-k workloads per team, which map cleanly onto other window functions like PERCENT_RANK or ROW_NUMBER.
